notes.front: What is an exhaust collector ring?
notes.back: A ring of thin corrosion-resistant steel tubing encircling a radial engine, collecting exhaust from each cylinder and ending at the tailpipe connection.
notes.explanation: It gathers the exhaust of every cylinder into one outlet instead of letting each cylinder exhaust separately.
notes.example: Like a gutter running round a roof, collecting from every downpipe and emptying at one corner.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Glossary, Glossary
notes.evidence: Collector ring. A ring made of thin corrosion-resistant steel tubing that encircles a radial engine and collects exhaust gases from each cylinder. The ring ends with a connection to the exhaust tail pipe.

notes.front: What is an exhaust augmentor (augmentor tube)?
notes.back: A long, specially shaped stainless steel tube around a reciprocating engine’s exhaust tailpipe that draws cooling air through the cylinder fins.
notes.explanation: Exhaust flowing through it produces a low pressure in the engine compartment, which pulls the cooling air in.
notes.example: Like a garden-hose sprayer that sucks in fertiliser as the water jet passes, but sucking in cooling air.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Glossary, Glossary
notes.evidence: Augmentor tube. A long, specially shaped stainless steel tube mounted around the exhaust tail pipe of a reciprocating engine. As exhaust gases flow through the augmentor tube, they produce a low pressure in the engine compartment that draws in cooling air through the cylinder fins.

notes.front: What does a turbine engine’s exhaust nozzle do to the gases leaving it?
notes.back: It acts as an orifice whose size determines the density and velocity of the gases as they emerge.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls this critical to thrust performance.
notes.example: Like the nozzle on a garden hose: its opening sets how fast and how dense the stream leaving it is.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Convergent Exhaust Nozzle”, p. 3-26
notes.evidence: In other words, the exhaust nozzle acts as an orifice, the size of which determines the density and velocity of the gases as they emerge from the engine. This is critical to thrust performance.

notes.front: What is a convergent exhaust nozzle?
notes.back: A nozzle whose cross-section decreases in the direction of flow, restricting the outlet so gas velocity and thrust increase.
notes.explanation: The first part of the nozzle and the exhaust plug form a divergent duct that reduces turbulence before the convergent part.
notes.example: Like squeezing the end of a hose so the water shoots out faster.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Convergent Exhaust Nozzle”, p. 3-26
notes.evidence: then the exhaust gases flow into the convergent component of the exhaust nozzle where the flow is restricted by a smaller outlet opening. Since this forms a convergent duct, the gas velocity is increased providing increased thrust.

notes.front: What is a convergent-divergent (C-D) exhaust nozzle?
notes.back: A nozzle that narrows to a throat and then widens, so gases reaching sonic speed at the throat keep accelerating as supersonic flow.
notes.explanation: The convergent part handles subsonic gas; the divergent part accelerates it further once it is supersonic.
notes.example: Like the convergent nozzle, but with a flared bell added after the narrowest point, as on rockets.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Convergent-Divergent Exhaust Nozzle”, p. 3-26
notes.evidence: In the convergent-divergent, or C-D nozzle, the convergent section is designed to handle the gases while they remain subsonic, and to deliver the gases to the throat of the nozzle just as they attain sonic velocity.

notes.front: What does a clamshell (mechanical-blockage) thrust reverser do?
notes.back: It places a barrier in the path of escaping exhaust gases, nullifying and reversing the engine’s forward thrust.
notes.explanation: Thrust reversers help stop heavy aircraft landing at high speeds, where brakes alone may not suffice.
notes.example: Like cupping a hand behind a hairdryer so the air blows back towards you.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Thrust Reversers”, p. 3-27
notes.evidence: The clamshell-type or mechanicalblockage reverser operates to form a barrier in the path of escaping exhaust gases, which nullifies and reverses the forward thrust of the engine.

notes.front: What is an afterburner?
notes.back: A component in a turbojet or turbofan exhaust system that increases thrust for take-off and special flight conditions.
notes.explanation: Much of the air through a gas turbine is used only for cooling, so it still holds enough oxygen to burn extra fuel.
notes.example: Like a second burner lit in a chimney, using the oxygen the first fire did not consume.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Glossary, Glossary
notes.evidence: Afterburner. A component in the exhaust system of a turbojet or turbofan engine used to increase the thrust for takeoff and for special flight conditions. Since much of the air passing through a gas turbine engine is used only for cooling, it still contains a great deal of oxygen.

notes.front: What is thrust vectoring?
notes.back: Directing an engine’s thrust other than parallel to the aircraft’s longitudinal axis by moving or repositioning the exhaust nozzle.
notes.explanation: Vertical take-off aircraft use it for lift-off, and military aircraft use it to manoeuvre.
notes.example: Like swivelling an outboard motor to steer a boat, rather than using a rudder.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Thrust Vectoring”, p. 3-29
notes.evidence: Thrust vectoring is the ability of an aircraft’s main engines to direct thrust other than parallel to the vehicle’s longitudinal axis, allowing the exhaust nozzle to move or change position to direct the thrust in varied directions.

notes.front: What is a turbine engine noise suppressor?
notes.back: A device, commonly an integral part of the engine installation or exhaust nozzle, that reduces exhaust noise.
notes.explanation: Such suppression is sometimes required at airports in or near highly populated areas.
notes.example: Like a car silencer, but shaped to break a jet stream into smaller jets.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Engine Noise Suppression”, p. 3-29
notes.evidence: Several types of noise suppressors are used. A common type of noise suppressor is an integral, airborne part of the aircraft engine installation or engine exhaust nozzle.

notes.front: Under which knowledge element do the Airman Certification Standards list hush kits?
notes.back: Noise suppression theory, components and operation, alongside mufflers and augmenter tubes.
notes.explanation: The standards name hush kits only as an example of noise suppression components.
notes.example: Like a muffler or augmenter tube, a hush kit belongs to the family of noise suppression components.
notes.source: FAA-S-ACS-1, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (2021), Section III, Subject L, Engine Exhaust and Reverser Systems, p. 58
notes.evidence: AM.III.L.K3 Noise suppression theory, components, and operation (e.g., mufflers, hush kits, augmenter tubes).

notes.front: Which gas turbine exhaust emissions does the handbook say most need lowering?
notes.back: Oxides of nitrogen (NOx), whose reduction continues to require improvement.
notes.explanation: Most research has centred on the combustion section of the engine.
notes.example: Like a car’s tailpipe emissions, with NOx the pollutant engineers work hardest to cut.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbine Engine Emissions”, p. 3-31
notes.evidence: Lowering exhaust emissions from gas turbine, especially oxides of nitrogen (NOX), continue to require improvement. Most of the research has centered around the combustion section of the engine.

notes.front: Where are short stack (open) exhaust systems used, compared with collector systems?
notes.back: Short stacks: nonsupercharged and low-powered engines where noise is not too objectionable. Collectors: most large nonsupercharged and all turbosupercharged engines.
notes.explanation: Collectors are also used where they improve nacelle streamlining or ease maintenance.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Exhaust Systems”, p. 3-21
notes.evidence: The short stack system is generally used on nonsupercharged engines and low-powered engines where noise level is not too objectionable. The collector system is used on most large nonsupercharged engines and on all turbosupercharged engines

notes.front: An engine is being fitted with a turbosupercharger. Which type of exhaust system must it have?
notes.back: C) A collector system, since the exhaust must be gathered to drive the turbine
notes.choices:
A) Short stacks, to keep back pressure low
B) Either type, as the turbine is gear-driven
C) A collector system, since the exhaust must be gathered to drive the turbine
D) No exhaust system, as the turbine takes all the gas
notes.choicesExplained: A cannot feed the turbine. B is wrong: a turbocharger is exhaust-driven. D is wrong: the gas still leaves through the tailpipe.
notes.explanation: The collector raises back pressure, but the handbook says the turbosupercharging gain more than offsets the loss.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Exhaust Systems”, p. 3-21
notes.evidence: On turbosupercharged engines, the exhaust gases must be collected to drive the turbine compressor of the supercharger.

notes.front: When an augmentor vane is fully closed, the tailpipe cross-sectional area is reduced by approximately {{c1::45 percent}}.
notes.explanation: Moving the vanes towards closed slows flow through the augmentor, raising engine temperature.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Manifold & Augmentor Exhaust Assembly”, p. 3-22
notes.evidence: When the vane is fully closed, the cross-sectional area of the tailpipe is reduced by approximately 45 percent.

notes.front: An augmentor tube that contains no heat exchanger surfaces shows a crack. Why must it still be dealt with?
notes.back: D) Cracks can let exhaust gases into the nacelle, wing or cabin, a fire or carbon monoxide hazard
notes.choices:
A) It need not be: only heat exchanger surfaces matter
B) Only because it lowers cooling slightly
C) Only because it spoils the tube’s appearance
D) Cracks can let exhaust gases into the nacelle, wing or cabin, a fire or carbon monoxide hazard
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the handbook says such tubes are still inspected for cracks. C and B ignore the fire and carbon monoxide hazard.
notes.explanation: Augmentor tubes should be inspected at regular intervals for alignment, security and condition, and for cracks.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Augmentor Exhaust System”, p. 3-24
notes.evidence: Even where augmentor tubes do not contain heat exchanger surfaces, they should be inspected for cracks along with the remainder of the exhaust system. Cracks in augmentor tubes can present a fire or carbon monoxide hazard by allowing exhaust gases to enter the nacelle, wing, or cabin areas.

notes.front: What can a reciprocating engine exhaust system failure lead to?
notes.back: Carbon monoxide poisoning of crew and passengers, partial or complete loss of engine power, or an aircraft fire.
notes.explanation: For this reason the handbook says any exhaust failure should be regarded as a severe hazard.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Exhaust System Maintenance Practices”, p. 3-22
notes.evidence: Any exhaust system failure should be regarded as a severe hazard. Depending on the location and type of failure, an exhaust system failure can result in carbon monoxide poisoning of crew and passengers, partial or complete loss of engine power, or an aircraft fire.

notes.front: A mechanic needs to mark an exhaust stack before removing it. Which marker does AC 43.13-1B allow?
notes.back: D) Chalk, Prussian blue, India ink or a carbon-free grease pencil
notes.choices:
A) A scribe mark from a galvanised tool
B) An ordinary lead pencil
C) A carbon-based pencil, if pressed lightly
D) Chalk, Prussian blue, India ink or a carbon-free grease pencil
notes.choicesExplained: B and C deposit carbon that causes cracks. A is wrong: galvanised or zinc-plated tools must never be used on exhaust systems.
notes.explanation: Carbon from pencils causes cracks through heat concentration and carbonisation; the handbook adds that lead, zinc or galvanised marks soften the metal.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Inspection and Repair, Chapter 8, Section 3, Exhaust Systems, par. 8-49, p. 8-33
notes.evidence: Carbon deposited by those tools will cause cracks from heat concentration and carbonization of the metal. If exhaust system parts must be marked, use chalk, Prussian blue, India ink, or a grease pencil that is carbon-free.

notes.front: Why must galvanised or zinc-plated tools and lead pencils never be used on exhaust parts?
notes.back: The lead, zinc or galvanised mark is absorbed into the hot metal, softening it and causing cracks and eventual failure.
notes.explanation: The absorbed mark changes the metal’s molecular structure where it was made.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust System Inspection”, p. 3-23
notes.evidence: The lead, zinc, or galvanized mark is absorbed by the metal of the exhaust system when heated, creating a distinct change in its molecular structure. This change softens the metal in the area of the mark, causing cracks and eventual failure.

notes.front: After a complete exhaust system and cowling are installed, how is it checked for leaks?
notes.back: Run the engine to normal operating temperatures, shut down, remove the cowling, and inspect every clamped and port connection.
notes.explanation: Heating the system to operating temperature shows leaks that a cold check might not.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust System Inspection”, p. 3-23
notes.evidence: After the installation of a complete exhaust system and all pieces of engine cowl are installed and secured, the engine should be operated to allow the exhaust system to heat up to normal operating temperatures.

notes.front: A flat grey streak marks a clamped exhaust joint. After repositioning the parts, tightening to the specified torque still leaves looseness. What next?
notes.back: B) Replace the bolts and nuts, which have probably stretched, then safety them
notes.choices:
A) Exceed the specified torque until it is tight
B) Replace the bolts and nuts, which have probably stretched, then safety them
C) Fit a thicker used gasket
D) Weld the joint solid
notes.choicesExplained: A breaks the torque limit. D is not the handbook’s remedy for a loose joint. C is wrong: old gaskets should never be reused.
notes.explanation: A leak usually comes from poor alignment of two mating parts, so they are repositioned first.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust System Inspection”, p. 3-23
notes.evidence: If tightening to the specified torque does not eliminate looseness, the bolts and nuts should be replaced since they have probably stretched. After tightening to the specified torque, all nuts should be safetied.

notes.front: How is an exhaust leak shown on the pipes, and what usually causes it?
notes.back: A flat grey or sooty black streak near the leak; usually poor alignment of two mated exhaust members.
notes.explanation: Black soot around an exhaust gasket likewise shows that the gasket has failed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust System Inspection”, p. 3-23
notes.evidence: An exhaust leak is indicated by a flat gray or a sooty black streak on the pipes in the area of the leak. An exhaust leak is usually the result of poor alignment of two mated exhaust system members.

notes.front: Ceramic-coated exhaust stacks need cleaning before inspection. What method should be used?
notes.back: B) Degreasing only
notes.choices:
A) Sandblasting
B) Degreasing only
C) An alkali cleaner
D) Wire brushing with a galvanised brush
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are expressly ruled out for ceramic-coated stacks. D brings a galvanised tool to the exhaust system, which must never be done.
notes.explanation: Some stacks have a plain sandblast finish, but ceramic-coated ones must never be sandblasted or cleaned with alkali.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust System Inspection”, p. 3-23
notes.evidence: Ceramiccoated stacks should be cleaned by degreasing only. They should never be cleaned with sandblast or alkali cleaners.

notes.front: What should dented areas or low spots in an exhaust system be checked for, and with what?
notes.back: Thinning and pitting from internal erosion by combustion products or moisture, probed with an ice pick or similar pointed tool.
notes.explanation: The system is disassembled as necessary to inspect internal baffles or diffusers.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust System Inspection”, p. 3-23
notes.evidence: Any dented areas or low spots in the system should be inspected for thinning and pitting due to internal erosion by combustion products or accumulated moisture. An ice pick or similar pointed instrument is useful in probing suspected areas.

notes.front: A muffler is hidden behind non-removable parts and cannot be fully inspected by eye. How does AC 43.13-1B say to check it for leaks?
notes.back: A) Remove it, plug its openings, apply about 2 psi internally and submerge it in water to look for bubbles
notes.choices:
A) Remove it, plug its openings, apply about 2 psi internally and submerge it in water to look for bubbles
B) Tap it with a hammer and listen for rattles only
C) Pressurise it in place to 20 psi with the engine running
D) Accept it if no soot is visible on the cowling
notes.choicesExplained: C uses neither the method nor the pressure in the AC. B would not find leaks. D skips the check the AC requires for an inaccessible component.
notes.explanation: AC 43.13-1B adds that the part must be dried thoroughly before reinstallation.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Inspection and Repair, Chapter 8, Section 3, Exhaust Systems, par. 8-49, p. 8-35
notes.evidence: remove the component and check for possible leaks by plugging its openings, applying approximately 2 psi internal pressure, and submerging it in water. Any leaks will cause bubbles that can be readily detected. Dry thoroughly before reinstallation.

notes.front: Why must ignition leads, hoses, fuel lines and flexible air ducts be protected near an exhaust system?
notes.back: The exhaust often runs red-hot at 1,000 °F or more; heat shields or adequate clearance protect them from radiated and convected heat.
notes.explanation: Inspectors also check that no part of the exhaust is chafed by cowling or control cables.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Inspection and Repair, Chapter 8, Section 3, Exhaust Systems, par. 8-49, p. 8-33
notes.evidence: The exhaust system often operates at red-hot temperatures of 1,000 °F or more; therefore, parts such as ignition leads, hoses, fuel lines, and flexible air ducts should be protected from radiation and convection heating by heat shields or adequate clearance.

notes.front: Approximately {{c1::half}} of all muffler and heat exchanger failures are traced to cracks or ruptures in heat exchanger surfaces used for cabin and carburettor heat.
notes.explanation: Failures in the heat exchanger surface, usually the outer wall, let exhaust gases escape straight into the cabin heat system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Muffler & Heat Exchanger Failures”, p. 3-23
notes.evidence: Approximately half of all muffler and heat exchanger failures can be traced to cracks or ruptures in the heat exchanger surfaces used for cabin and carburetor heat sources.

notes.front: Besides the carbon monoxide hazard, what can a failed heat exchanger surface do to the engine?
notes.back: Let exhaust gases be drawn into the induction system, causing engine overheating and power loss.
notes.explanation: These failures are mostly thermal and vibration fatigue cracks in areas of stress concentration.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Muffler & Heat Exchanger Failures”, p. 3-24
notes.evidence: In addition to a carbon monoxide hazard, failure of heat exchanger surfaces can permit exhaust gases to be drawn into the engine induction system, causing engine overheating and power loss.

notes.front: A pilot reports headaches and drowsiness on flights with the cabin heat on. Which exhaust fault fits best?
notes.back: B) A crack in the muffler’s heat exchanger surface letting exhaust into the cabin heat system
notes.choices:
A) A loose baffle blocking the muffler outlet
B) A crack in the muffler’s heat exchanger surface letting exhaust into the cabin heat system
C) Coke in the turbocharger
D) An augmentor vane stuck in trail
notes.choicesExplained: A causes power loss by restricting exhaust flow. C causes gradual power loss. D affects engine cooling, not cabin air.
notes.explanation: Heat exchanger surface failures, usually in the outer wall, let exhaust gas escape directly into the cabin heat.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Muffler & Heat Exchanger Failures”, p. 3-23
notes.evidence: Failures in the heat exchanger surface (usually in the outer wall) allow

notes.front: Where do exhaust manifold and stack failures usually occur, and what hazard do they chiefly present?
notes.back: As fatigue failures at welded or clamped points; they are primarily fire hazards, though they also present carbon monoxide problems.
notes.explanation: Exhaust can reach the cabin through poor seals at firewall openings, wing strut fittings, doors and wing roots.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust Manifold & Stack Failures”, p. 3-24
notes.evidence: Exhaust manifold and stack failures are usually fatigue failures at welded or clamped points (e.g., stack-to-flange, stack-to-manifold, and crossover pipe or muffler connections). Although these failures are primarily fire hazards, they also present carbon monoxide problems.

notes.front: Inspection finds a fatigue crack at a stack-to-flange weld. What type of failure is this, and what is its main hazard?
notes.back: B) A manifold and stack failure, primarily a fire hazard
notes.choices:
A) An internal muffler failure, primarily a power-loss hazard
B) A manifold and stack failure, primarily a fire hazard
C) A heat exchanger failure, primarily an induction icing hazard
D) A thrust reverser failure
notes.choicesExplained: A concerns baffles and diffusers inside the muffler. C misstates the heat exchanger hazard. D belongs to turbine engines.
notes.explanation: Manifold and stack failures also present carbon monoxide problems if exhaust reaches the cabin.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust Manifold & Stack Failures”, p. 3-24
notes.evidence: Exhaust gases can enter the cabin via defective or inadequate seals at firewall openings, wing strut fittings, doors, and wing root openings.

notes.front: What are the primary causes of internal muffler failures, and what can they do to the engine?
notes.back: Erosion and carburisation from extreme heat; loose baffles can restrict or block exhaust flow, causing partial or complete power loss.
notes.explanation: Backfiring and combustion of unburned fuel in the exhaust are probable contributing factors.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Internal Muffler Failures”, p. 3-24
notes.evidence: As opposed to other failures, erosion and carburization caused by the extreme thermal conditions are the primary causes of internal failures. Engine backfiring and combustion of unburned fuel within the exhaust system are probable contributing factors.

notes.front: An engine has twice lost power with high back pressure, traced to broken muffler baffles blocking the outlet. What does AC 43.13-1B suggest, beyond replacing the muffler?
notes.back: A) Install an exhaust outlet guard, while still inspecting the muffler internals
notes.choices:
A) Install an exhaust outlet guard, while still inspecting the muffler internals
B) Remove the internal baffles altogether
C) Weld the loose baffle pieces to the outlet
D) Enlarge the outlet with protruding weld beads
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are not AC remedies. D is wrong: protruding weld beads cause hot spots and restrict flow.
notes.explanation: The guard does not remove the need for thorough inspection of internal parts or replacement of defective mufflers.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Inspection and Repair, Chapter 8, Section 3, Exhaust Systems, par. 8-48, p. 8-32
notes.evidence: Engine power loss and excessive backpressure caused by exhaust outlet blockage may be averted by the installation of an exhaust outlet guard as shown in Figures 8-21a and 8-21b.

notes.front: A turbocharged engine shows manifold pressure above its limits. Inspection finds heavy carbon build-up in the waste gate unit. What has probably happened?
notes.back: A) The deposits have made the waste gate stick closed, causing overboost
notes.choices:
A) The deposits have made the waste gate stick closed, causing overboost
B) The deposits have cooled the exhaust
C) The exhaust has become too quiet
D) The waste gate has stuck open, cutting boost
notes.choicesExplained: D would reduce boost, not raise it. B and C are not effects the handbook describes.
notes.explanation: The handbook says periodic de-coking has proved necessary, and turbo exhaust systems run at greatly increased pressure and temperature.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust Systems with Turbocharger”, p. 3-24
notes.evidence: A common cause of malfunction is coke deposits (carbon buildup) in the waste gate unit causing erratic system operation. Excessive deposit buildups may cause the waste gate valve to stick in the “closed” position, causing an overboost condition.

notes.front: What is generally recommended for defective exhaust stacks, mufflers and tailpipes, and why are welded repairs difficult?
notes.back: Replacement with new or reconditioned parts; identifying the base metal for the right repair materials is difficult.
notes.explanation: Changes in the base metal’s composition and grain structure complicate welding further.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust System Repairs”, p. 3-24
notes.evidence: It is generally recommended that exhaust stacks, mufflers, tailpipes, etc., be replaced with new or reconditioned components rather than repaired. Welded repairs to exhaust systems are complicated by the difficulty of accurately identifying the base metal so that the proper repair materials can be selected.

notes.front: Why are repairs or weld beads that protrude inside an exhaust pipe not acceptable?
notes.back: They cause local hot spots and may restrict exhaust gas flow.
notes.explanation: Welded repairs must also keep the original contours and not warp the system’s alignment.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust System Repairs”, p. 3-24
notes.evidence: Repairs or sloppy weld beads that protrude internally are not acceptable as they cause local hot spots and may restrict exhaust gas flow.

notes.front: During exhaust reassembly, the special high-temperature locknuts are out of stock and the old gaskets look usable. What is acceptable?
notes.back: B) Neither: use the manufacturer’s high-temperature locknuts and new gaskets of the same type
notes.choices:
A) Fit steel self-locking nuts and reuse the old gaskets
B) Neither: use the manufacturer’s high-temperature locknuts and new gaskets of the same type
C) Fit low-temperature self-locking nuts and new gaskets
D) Reuse the gaskets but order the correct nuts
notes.choicesExplained: A and C substitute nuts the handbook forbids. A and D reuse gaskets, which should never be done.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the proper hardware and clamps should always be used on exhaust systems.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust System Repairs”, p. 3-24
notes.evidence: Steel or low temperature, self-locking nuts should not be substituted for brass or special high temperature locknuts used by the manufacturer. Old gaskets should never be re-used.

notes.front: How do ducted-fan and unducted-fan turbofans differ at the exhaust?
notes.back: Ducted fans mix fan and core flow in a common exhaust nozzle; unducted fans have separate nozzles for fan and core airflow.
notes.explanation: In the separate-nozzle engine, fan air creates most of the thrust.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbine Engine Exhaust Nozzles”, p. 3-25
notes.evidence: Then, it flows into a common exhaust nozzle. The core exhaust flow and the fan flow mix and flow from the engine through this mixed nozzle. The unducted fan has two nozzles, one for the fan airflow and one for the core airflow.

notes.front: An engine’s exhaust nozzle provides only about 10–15 percent of total thrust and mainly discharges the gases, most energy having gone to a propeller. What engine is it?
notes.back: D) A turboprop
notes.choices:
A) A ducted-fan turbofan
B) A turbojet with afterburner
C) A helicopter turboshaft with a divergent nozzle
D) A turboprop
notes.choicesExplained: B gets its thrust from the exhaust jet. C’s divergent nozzle provides no thrust. A gets most thrust from fan air through the mixed nozzle.
notes.explanation: A helicopter turboshaft nozzle may give no thrust at all, while a separate-nozzle turbofan’s fan provides 80–85 percent.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbine Engine Exhaust Nozzles”, p. 3-25
notes.evidence: Turboprop exhaust nozzles provide small amounts of thrust (10–15 percent) but are mainly used to discharge the exhaust gases from the aircraft. Most of the energy has been transferred to the propeller.

notes.front: What goes wrong if a convergent exhaust nozzle’s opening is too big or too small?
notes.back: Too big wastes thrust; too small chokes the flow in the other engine components.
notes.explanation: Adjusting nozzle area changes both engine performance and exhaust gas temperature.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Convergent Exhaust Nozzle”, p. 3-26
notes.evidence: The restriction of the opening of the outlet of the exhaust nozzle is limited by two factors. If the nozzle opening is too big, thrust is being wasted. If it is too little, the flow is choked in the other components of the engine.

notes.front: An engine’s pressure ratio is high enough that exhaust velocity might exceed Mach 1 at the nozzle. Which nozzle gains more thrust?
notes.back: D) A convergent-divergent nozzle
notes.choices:
A) A convergent nozzle, choked at Mach 1
B) A divergent-only duct, as on helicopters
C) A multi-tube noise suppressor
D) A convergent-divergent nozzle
notes.choicesExplained: A’s flow stays at Mach 1 at the opening once choked. B gives no thrust. C is a noise suppressor, not a thrust nozzle.
notes.explanation: Its advantage is greatest at high Mach numbers, because of the higher pressure ratio across the nozzle.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Convergent-Divergent Exhaust Nozzle”, p. 3-26
notes.evidence: Whenever the engine pressure ratio is high enough to produce exhaust gas velocities which might exceed Mach 1 at the engine exhaust nozzle, more thrust can be gained by using a convergent-divergent type of nozzle.

notes.front: Why have thrust reversers become necessary on many aircraft?
notes.back: Heavier aircraft with higher landing speeds are harder to stop, and brakes often can no longer be relied on alone.
notes.explanation: Reversers help slow the aircraft within a reasonable distance immediately after touchdown.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Thrust Reversers”, p. 3-27
notes.evidence: In many instances, the aircraft brakes can no longer be relied upon solely to slow the aircraft within a reasonable distance, immediately after touchdown.

notes.front: How does a mechanical-blockage thrust reverser differ from an aerodynamic-blockage type?
notes.back: Mechanical blockage puts an obstruction in the exhaust, generally on ducted turbofans; aerodynamic blockage redirects only fan air, mainly on unducted turbofans.
notes.explanation: Mechanical blockage uses an inverted cone, half-sphere or clamshell; aerodynamic uses blocker doors and cascade vanes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Thrust Reversers”, p. 3-27
notes.evidence: In the aerodynamic blockage type of thrust reverser, used mainly with unducted turbofan engines, only fan air is used to slow the aircraft.

notes.front: A reverser has a translating cowl that opens as blocker doors close, turning fan air forward through cascade vanes. Which category is it?
notes.back: A) Aerodynamic blockage
notes.choices:
A) Aerodynamic blockage
B) Mechanical blockage (clamshell)
C) Thrust vectoring
D) Afterburning
notes.choicesExplained: B places an obstruction behind the nozzle. C redirects thrust in flight by moving the nozzle. D adds thrust rather than reversing it.
notes.explanation: Since the fan can produce about 80 percent of the thrust, the fan is the best source of reverse thrust.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Thrust Reversers”, p. 3-27
notes.evidence: A modern aerodynamic thrust reverser system consists of a translating cowl, blocker doors, and cascade vanes that redirect the fan airflow to slow the aircraft.

notes.front: In the handbook’s aerodynamic reverser, what conditions apply when the thrust levers are moved aft to deploy it?
notes.back: The thrust levers are at idle and the aircraft has weight on its wheels.
notes.explanation: Returning the levers to idle opens the blocker doors and closes the translating cowl.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Thrust Reversers”, p. 3-27
notes.evidence: If the thrust levers are at idle position and the aircraft has weight on the wheels, moving the thrust levers aft activates the translating cowl to open, closing the blocker doors.

notes.front: A mechanic is about to work inside the thrust reverser area of a turbofan. What must be done first?
notes.back: A) Mechanically lock the reverser out from deploying while people are in the area
notes.choices:
A) Mechanically lock the reverser out from deploying while people are in the area
B) Stow the thrust levers at idle
C) Rely on the flight deck reverser indication
D) Nothing, as reversers deploy only in flight
notes.choicesExplained: D is wrong: reversers deploy on the ground. B and C do not mechanically prevent deployment.
notes.explanation: Reversers have many moving parts, powered pneumatically or hydraulically, so maintenance and inspection requirements are very important.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Thrust Reversers”, p. 3-27
notes.evidence: Since there are several moving parts, maintenance and inspection requirements are very important. While performing any type of maintenance, the reverser system must be mechanically locked out from deploying while personnel are in the area of the reverser system.

notes.front: What somewhat limits operation in afterburner mode?
notes.back: High fuel consumption, which can be almost double normal consumption.
notes.explanation: Because fuel is burned in the exhaust nozzle, heat build-up there is also a problem, handled by a special liner.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Afterburning/Thrust Augmentation”, p. 3-29
notes.evidence: Operation in the afterburner mode is somewhat limited by high fuel consumption, which can be almost double normal consumption.

notes.front: In the handbook’s example, the pilot can vector the nozzle up and down by {{c1::20°}}, making the aircraft much more manoeuvrable.
notes.explanation: Usually the nozzle points straight out of the engine.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Thrust Vectoring”, p. 3-29
notes.evidence: Usually, the nozzle points straight out of the engine. The pilot can move, or vector, the vectoring nozzle up and down by 20°.

notes.front: Why is low-frequency jet exhaust noise more objectionable on the ground than high-frequency noise?
notes.back: The lower the frequency, the farther it travels, so it reaches people in greater volume.
notes.explanation: High-frequency noise is weakened faster by distance, buildings, terrain and atmospheric disturbances.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Engine Noise Suppression”, p. 3-30
notes.evidence: This means that the low-frequency noises reach an individual on the ground in greater volume than the high-frequency noises, and hence are more objectionable.

notes.front: How do corrugated-perimeter and multi-tube noise suppressors reduce noise?
notes.back: They break the jet into smaller streams, raising the frequency, which the atmosphere absorbs more or which may exceed hearing range.
notes.explanation: The total noise energy is unchanged; only its frequency is raised.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Engine Noise Suppression”, p. 3-30
notes.evidence: Both types of suppressors break up the single, main jet exhaust stream into a number of smaller jet streams. This increases the total perimeter of the nozzle area and reduces the size of the air stream eddies created as the gases are discharged into the open air.

notes.front: Which of these changes would the handbook expect to lower jet engine noise at a noise-sensitive airport?
notes.back: C) Operating at lower power settings, or using a turbofan version of the engine
notes.choices:
A) Raising turbine discharge temperature
B) Using a smaller engine at full thrust instead of a larger one at part thrust
C) Operating at lower power settings, or using a turbofan version of the engine
D) Selecting afterburner for a shorter take-off
notes.choicesExplained: B is backwards: large engines at partial thrust are quieter. A and D raise jet velocity and so noise.
notes.explanation: Noise is proportional to exhaust gas velocity, and a turbofan’s exhaust is slower than a comparable turbojet’s.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Engine Noise Suppression”, p. 3-30
notes.evidence: Thus, the noise level can be reduced considerably by operating the engine at lower power settings. Compared with a turbojet, a turbofan version of the same engine is quieter during takeoff.

notes.front: How does the Twin Annular, Pre-mixing Swirler combustor design reduce NOx?
notes.back: Swirlers make a more thorough, leaner fuel-air mix that burns at lower temperatures.
notes.explanation: Most NOx forms when oxygen and nitrogen react at high temperatures, and more so the longer the mixture stays hot.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbine Engine Emissions”, p. 3-31
notes.evidence: This swirl creates a more thorough and leaner mix of fuel and air, which burns at lower temperatures than in previous gas turbine engine designs. Most of the NOX is formed by the reaction of oxygen and nitrogen at high temperatures.
